name: The Waste Land
kicker: T. S. Eliot’s 1922 modernist poem · Reinvented English poetry out of fragments
briefing: T. S. Eliot’s _The Waste Land_ (1922) reads like a radio dial spinning through a ruined world: a tarot reading, a London pub at closing time, a boat on the Thames, and lines in German, French, and Sanskrit all crash together without warning. Eliot’s friend Ezra Pound cut the original draft nearly in half. The poem opens by mocking springtime itself — “April is the cruellest month” — and ends, just as suddenly, with a Sanskrit word for peace said three times.

sample.note: the 13 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (1 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This poem’s epigraph, from Petronius’ _Satyricon_, quotes the Sibyl of Cumae saying that she wants to die. Ezra Pound cut the original draft of this poem nearly in half, and it is dedicated to him as “the better craftsman.” A fortune-teller named Madame Sosostris deals out a tarot card showing a drowned sailor.
tossups.r: That sailor, Phlebas the Phoenician, gets his own short section called “Death by Water.” For 10 points, name this five-part modernist poem that opens “April is the cruellest month,” written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: The blind prophet Tiresias, who has lived as both a man and a woman, narrates this poem’s scene of a bored typist and a pimply young clerk. This poem repeatedly calls a fog-choked London the “Unreal City.” A one-eyed merchant named Mr. Eugenides invites this poem’s narrator to lunch at the Cannon Street Hotel.
tossups.r: This poem’s final section has thunder repeat three commands from the Upanishads: “Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.” For 10 points, name this modernist poem that ends with the Sanskrit chant “Shantih shantih shantih,” written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: A character named Marie recalls being told to “hold on tight” while sledding in this poem’s first section, “The Burial of the Dead.” Much later, this poem asks, “Who is the third who walks always beside you?” In its second section, a bartender’s call of “HURRY UP PLEASE IT’S TIME” interrupts a pub conversation about a woman named Lil’s false teeth.
tossups.r: That section is titled “A Game of Chess.” For 10 points, name this fragmented modernist poem by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem’s first section quotes a German-language line, “Bin gar keine Russin,” and mentions a trip to the Hofgarten. A nightingale’s song is rendered as “Jug jug” after a description of people washing their feet in soda water. This poem’s narrator also asks a war veteran named Stetson whether a corpse has “begun to sprout.”
tossups.r: This poem’s final section quotes the nursery rhyme “London Bridge is falling down.” For 10 points, name this modernist poem that begins “April is the cruellest month,” by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem’s closing lines quote “Hieronymo’s mad againe” from Thomas Kyd’s _The Spanish Tragedy_, part of a jumble of quotations in several languages. Earlier, this poem describes Mrs. Porter and her daughter washing their feet in soda water in a section called “The Fire Sermon.” A tense, one-sided conversation in this poem includes the line “I think we are in rats’ alley.”
tossups.r: This poem’s fortune-teller, Madame Sosostris, reads a tarot card showing a drowned Phoenician sailor. For 10 points, name this T. S. Eliot poem that ends with the Sanskrit words “Shantih shantih shantih.”

tossups.p: A one-eyed merchant from Smyrna named Mr. Eugenides invites this poem’s narrator to lunch at the Cannon Street Hotel. Later in the same section, the blind prophet Tiresias watches a bored typist return home to be visited by a “young man carbuncular.” This poem’s third section is titled “The Fire Sermon.”
tossups.r: This poem’s first section describes Madame Sosostris dealing tarot cards, including one showing Phlebas the Phoenician. For 10 points, name this modernist poem by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem’s line “I will show you fear in a handful of dust” later gave Evelyn Waugh the title for one of his novels. Near its end, this poem quotes the nursery rhyme “London Bridge is falling down” among fragments in English, French, Italian, and Sanskrit. This poem’s narrator receives a lunch invitation from a Smyrna merchant, Mr. Eugenides.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this modernist poem that opens by calling April “the cruellest month,” written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: In this poem, a tense exchange includes the line “I think we are in rats’ alley / Where the dead men lost their bones.” That conversation appears in the same section where a woman named Lil is urged to get false teeth before her husband Albert returns. A bartender’s repeated cry of “HURRY UP PLEASE IT’S TIME” keeps interrupting the talk about Lil.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this five-section poem, whose final section, “What the Thunder Said,” ends with a Sanskrit chant, written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem describes Mrs. Porter and her daughter washing their feet in soda water in its third section, “The Fire Sermon.” That section is narrated in part by Tiresias, a blind prophet who has lived as both a man and a woman. This poem’s narrator is invited to lunch at the Cannon Street Hotel by a merchant named Mr. Eugenides.
tossups.r: This poem ends with three commands from the Upanishads — “Datta,” “Dayadhvam,” “Damyata” — followed by a Sanskrit peace chant. For 10 points, name this poem by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem’s narrator asks a fellow war veteran named Stetson whether a corpse planted in his garden has “begun to sprout.” This poem repeatedly describes a fog-bound London as an “Unreal City.” Its first section, “The Burial of the Dead,” also features a fortune-teller named Madame Sosostris reading tarot cards.
tossups.r: One of those cards shows a drowned sailor named Phlebas the Phoenician. For 10 points, name this modernist poem that begins “April is the cruellest month,” written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem is split into five sections, including “A Game of Chess” and “The Fire Sermon.” Its first section, “The Burial of the Dead,” introduces the fortune-teller Madame Sosostris, who deals tarot cards to the narrator, including one depicting a drowned Phoenician sailor. That sailor, Phlebas, later gets his own brief section titled “Death by Water.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this modernist poem, dedicated to Ezra Pound, that ends with the Sanskrit words “Shantih shantih shantih.”

tossups.p: Ezra Pound’s heavy editing cut this poem nearly in half, and it carries a dedication calling Pound “the better craftsman.” This poem’s epigraph, quoting Petronius’ _Satyricon_, has the Sibyl of Cumae say that she wants to die. Its first section describes a character named Marie recalling a childhood sledding trip.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this modernist poem whose final section, “What the Thunder Said,” ends with a thrice-repeated Sanskrit word for peace, written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: In its final section, thunder repeats three Sanskrit commands drawn from the Upanishads: “Datta,” “Dayadhvam,” and “Damyata.” That section, “What the Thunder Said,” also quotes the nursery rhyme “London Bridge is falling down.” Earlier, this poem’s blind prophet Tiresias narrates a scene between a typist and a “young man carbuncular.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, identify this modernist poem that ends with three repetitions of the Sanskrit word “Shantih,” written by T. S. Eliot.

tossups.p: This poem’s opening section slips into German with the line “Bin gar keine Russin,” recalling a visit to the Hofgarten. In a later section, a nightingale’s song becomes “Jug jug” after this poem describes a mother and daughter washing their feet in soda water. The first section also introduces Madame Sosostris, who reads the narrator’s tarot cards.
tossups.r: One of those cards depicts the drowned sailor Phlebas the Phoenician. For 10 points, name this T. S. Eliot poem, whose first section is titled “The Burial of the Dead.”

tossups.p: A merchant from Smyrna named Mr. Eugenides invites this poem’s narrator to lunch at the Cannon Street Hotel. This poem’s line “I will show you fear in a handful of dust” later lent its title to a novel by Evelyn Waugh. Its third section, narrated partly by the blind prophet Tiresias, is called “The Fire Sermon.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this modernist poem that begins by calling April “the cruellest month” and ends with a Sanskrit chant, written by T. S. Eliot.

trap.title: Which Eliot poem?
trap.body: T. S. Eliot wrote several famous poems, and quiz bowl loves to mix them up. “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” is a single speaker’s nervous monologue (“Do I dare to eat a peach?”). This poem is much bigger and louder: five sections, a whole cast of voices (Madame Sosostris, Tiresias, Mr. Eugenides), and lines in several languages.
trap.fix: Listen for the specific cast of characters — Madame Sosostris, Phlebas, Tiresias, Mr. Eugenides — or the sections “The Burial of the Dead” and “What the Thunder Said.” Prufrock clues mention a peach, mermaids, or “time for you and time for me,” never a tarot deck.
